cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: A Texas-sized iron asteroid is knocked out of the asteroid belt toward Earth by a comet collision.
cases.critique: No asteroid that big exists (Ceres is ~900 km, Texas ~1400 km) and a comet could not shove a ~5e24 g iron body out of its orbit: 'you could ram it with comets for years and not move it much.'
cases.status_reason: Ceres (~940 km) remains the largest main-belt body; momentum conservation makes a comet impact negligible for such a mass.
cases.game_note: The game has no asteroids or impact deflection; its bodies come from the star catalogue and planet models.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: The 'Texas-sized' asteroid is jagged and spiky.
cases.critique: A body that large is pulled into a sphere by its own gravity; a collision big enough to send it to Earth would have melted it round.
cases.status_reason: Bodies above a few hundred km (e.g. Ceres, Vesta near the limit) approach hydrostatic shapes; a 1000+ km body would be near-spherical, as Dawn confirmed for Ceres.
cases.game_note: The game does not depict small-body shapes; planet icons are stylised (6.9).

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: The cosmonaut spins the Russian space station to create gravity just before the shuttles dock.
cases.critique: A spinning station would be very hard to dock with, the small docking tube couldn't hold the shuttle against spin 'gravity', and the movie's 'gravity goes every which way'; at the hub there would be no force at all.
cases.status_reason: Centripetal pseudo-gravity points outward from the spin axis and vanishes at the hub; docking with a spinning body requires matching rotation.
cases.game_note: No docking or spin-station scenes; stations (8.1) are abstract population caps.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: A nuclear bomb splits the 1000-km asteroid four hours before impact so both halves miss Earth.
cases.critique: Each half would need ~1600 km/h sideways in 4 hours; for that mass this needs ~1e11 megatons, roughly the Sun's output per second - 'one bomb ain't gonna do it. A billion or so might.'
cases.status_reason: Simple kinetic-energy arithmetic; modern deflection studies (and NASA's 2022 DART test) emphasize years of lead time, not last-hour splitting.
cases.game_note: No asteroid deflection in the game; its energy bookkeeping concerns ships and swarms instead.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: On the asteroid, crew need thrusters to stay on the surface, yet inside the ship they walk normally.
cases.critique: 'The writers forgot that gravity can penetrate even the impenetrable titanium of the rocket's hull' - the pilot running inside should have launched herself into the walls.
cases.status_reason: Gravity cannot be shielded; the low surface gravity applies inside the lander too.
cases.game_note: The game never depicts gravity inside ships or on small bodies.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Astronauts walk and bounce on the 11-km comet as if in moderate gravity.
cases.critique: An 11-km comet has surface gravity ~1/10,000 of Earth's and escape velocity of a few m/s - an 80 kg astronaut would weigh ~12 g and could easily leap off.
cases.status_reason: Rosetta's Philae bounce on 67P (2014, escape speed ~1 m/s) dramatically confirmed how feeble comet gravity is.
cases.game_note: Surface gravity is computed as M/R^2 (7.10), so low-mass bodies correctly get feeble gravity.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: The comet surface is shown bright white/gray.
cases.critique: Comets are among the darkest objects in the solar system; Giotto found Halley's nucleus 'darker than coal', reflecting ~3-4% of light.
cases.status_reason: Later missions (Deep Impact/Tempel 1, Rosetta/67P with ~6% albedo) confirmed very dark nuclei.
cases.game_note: Albedo of small bodies is not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Before the tsunami hits, the water near the beach recedes dramatically.
cases.critique: Because the impact wave travels faster than sound, distant water would have 'no warning' and should not recede before the wave arrives (Plait later added a hedge after reader corrections).
cases.status_reason: Drawdown happens whenever a wave trough arrives first (as seen in the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami); impact-generated tsunamis are wave trains, so recession before a crest is plausible.
cases.game_note: Ocean wave behaviour is not part of the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Astronauts blow up the second comet fragment minutes before impact, saving Earth.
cases.critique: 'Blowing up a comet does no good at all' - if the pieces still hit, all the kinetic energy is still dumped into the atmosphere, dwarfing all nuclear arsenals combined.
cases.status_reason: Correct for a last-minute disruption, but recent planetary-defense work (e.g. 'pulverize it' fragmentation studies, 2020s) finds that breaking a body into small pieces with adequate lead time can spread energy so it is largely harmless.
cases.game_note: Fragmenting an impactor still delivers its kinetic energy; the game ignores that its own 0.9c fleets carry ~5e4 Chicxulubs each and never strike planets (5.2).

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: When the Machine activates its strong gravity field, ships in the harbor lean toward it.
cases.critique: Buoyancy keeps decks perpendicular to local gravity, so the ships should heel the other way, decks tilting away from the Machine (point credited to a reader, added 2001).
cases.status_reason: A floating hull aligns its deck with the local equipotential surface, i.e. normal to the net gravity vector.
cases.game_note: No such scene in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Ellie experiences ~18 hours in transit while zero time passes on Earth.
cases.critique: Even moving at relativistic or superluminal speed, her conversation with her 'father' takes time, so some time must elapse in Earth's frame; a zero-time trip 'won't work' without alien time manipulation.
cases.status_reason: Sound in principle (any nonzero proper time maps to nonzero external time along ordinary paths), but wormhole geometries can act as time machines (Morris-Thorne-Yurtsever 1988), so zero elapsed Earth time is exotic rather than strictly impossible.
cases.game_note: Like the film, the game never shows elapsed traveller (proper) time; trips are given only in Earth-frame years, and teams 'arriving at c' (2.8j) would imply zero proper time.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.work: Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace
cases.depiction: Ships are silhouetted against sunlit Naboo with a sky full of bright stars.
cases.critique: Contrast: a sunlit planet is thousands of times brighter than stars, so any exposure showing the planet properly would show no stars - you never see stars in shuttle footage of Earth.
cases.status_reason: Dynamic-range limits of eyes and cameras; ISS imagery still shows the same effect.
cases.game_note: No camera exposure is simulated; system views are maps, not photographs.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.work: Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace
cases.depiction: Tatooine orbits two suns of similar apparent size that set together.
cases.critique: Analyzes binary-star orbits: figure-8 orbits are unstable, an S-type orbit would make the far star look small, so the likely configuration is a stable circumbinary (P-type) orbit far outside both stars; also notes scenes show single shadows.
cases.status_reason: Kepler-16b (2011) and later circumbinary planets (Kepler-34b, -35b, TOI-1338b) confirmed exactly the stable P-type 'Tatooine' configuration he favored.
cases.game_note: Binary systems use a sep/3 stability cut and Kepler periods for companions, so planet orbits in binaries are treated sensibly.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.work: Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace
cases.depiction: Padme tells Anakin 'space is cold'.
cases.critique: Space itself has no temperature; a thermometer in space reads whatever radiation it absorbs - hot near a star, ~3 K far from any star because of the cosmic background.
cases.status_reason: Equilibrium temperature depends on radiative balance; CMB at 2.725 K sets the floor.
cases.game_note: Planet temperatures are equilibrium temperatures from stellar radiation, consistent with space having no temperature of its own.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.work: Star Wars: Episode II - Attack of the Clones
cases.depiction: Obi-Wan dogfights through Geonosis's dense ring of huge tumbling boulders.
cases.critique: Real ring particles (Saturn's) are at most a few meters; such a dense field of big rocks would grind itself to dust by collisions long ago.
cases.status_reason: Cassini (2004-2017) confirmed Saturn's ring particles are mostly cm-to-m sized with sparse spacing; collisional grinding limits sizes.
cases.game_note: No ring or asteroid fields are drawn (ring icons in 6.9 are iconography only).

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.work: Star Wars: Episode II - Attack of the Clones
cases.depiction: Jango Fett's seismic charges produce a booming shock wave in space.
cases.critique: Sound needs a medium; in vacuum there would be no sound and no blast wave.
cases.status_reason: No acoustic propagation in vacuum; debris ring gas is far too thin.
cases.game_note: The game has no audio and no explosion effects at all.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.work: Star Wars: Episode II - Attack of the Clones
cases.depiction: Count Dooku flies a solar-sail ship to a distant star system.
cases.critique: Light pressure gives tiny accelerations; sails are fine for interplanetary travel but crossing 'halfway across the galaxy' by sail would take thousands to hundreds of thousands of years.
cases.status_reason: IKAROS (2010) and LightSail 2 (2019) confirmed micro-newton-scale thrust; interstellar sails need laser beaming (e.g. Breakthrough Starshot concept).
cases.game_note: The game's laser sails reach 0.95c only via an idealised laser (fixed 0.8 beam efficiency, diffraction ignored, 4.9) and in G instantly (1.2).

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.work: Star Wars: Episode III - Revenge of the Sith
cases.depiction: After the cruiser loses artificial gravity, the corridor tilts and people slide down the floor as it falls toward the planet.
cases.critique: Falling under the planet's gravity, everything aboard accelerates equally, so without artificial gravity they should float, not slide - which is why orbiting astronauts float.
cases.status_reason: Equivalence principle: free-falling objects share the same acceleration (atmospheric drag later would add some deceleration).
cases.game_note: Ship interiors and falling ships are not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.work: Star Wars: Episode III - Revenge of the Sith
cases.depiction: The falling cruiser burns as it re-enters the atmosphere.
cases.critique: Points out re-entry heating is not mainly friction but compression of the air ahead of the ship (ram/shock heating).
cases.status_reason: Re-entry heating is dominated by shock-layer compression of gas ahead of the vehicle, with friction a minor contributor.
cases.game_note: No atmospheric entry is depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: An astronaut takes off his helmet in space and instantly freezes solid, his face distorting.
cases.critique: The body holds lots of heat and in vacuum can lose it only by slow radiation, so he would not freeze quickly; nor would he explode.
cases.status_reason: Vacuum-exposure data (e.g. 1966 NASA chamber accident) show unconsciousness in ~15 s but no instant freezing or explosion.
cases.game_note: No human exposure to vacuum in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Dr Pepper leaking through a meteoroid hole freezes in place almost instantly outside the hull.
cases.critique: The liquid wouldn't freeze so quickly: in vacuum heat can only be radiated away, 'a very inefficient and slow process.'
cases.status_reason: Liquid exposed to vacuum flash-boils and evaporative cooling freezes the remainder within seconds (as with shuttle/ISS water dumps forming ice crystals), so rapid freezing is realistic.
cases.game_note: No liquids in vacuum are depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Terri Fisher fires her suit jets for a long time chasing her husband, then gives only a brief burst to stop.
cases.critique: No friction in space: Newton's laws mean she must spend as much thrust stopping as she spent accelerating, so a short burst could not stop her.
cases.status_reason: Delta-v to stop equals delta-v gained; elementary Newtonian mechanics.
cases.game_note: Stopping needs as much delta-v as starting, yet G brakes instantly, S brakes a magsail at 1g, and redirects and waypoint turns are free.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: When power returns, the ship's spin wheels restore gravity instantly and everything drops to the floor.
cases.critique: Spin gravity can't switch on like a light: the wheels must spin up gradually, and objects floating inside wouldn't immediately 'fall' until the moving floor reaches them.
cases.status_reason: Centripetal pseudo-gravity scales with spin rate and only acts on objects co-rotating with the structure.
cases.game_note: No spin-gravity habitats are modelled.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: The ship uses two counter-rotating gravity wheels; a fire extinguisher's spray pushes Bowman backwards.
cases.critique: Praises both: counter-rotating wheels cancel angular momentum so the ship itself doesn't spin, and extinguisher recoil in weightlessness is accurate.
cases.status_reason: Angular momentum and momentum conservation, standard design practice for spin habitats.
cases.game_note: No spin-gravity habitats are modelled.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Astronauts on Mars stand against a pinkish-orange sky.
cases.critique: Close: suspended dust makes the Martian daytime sky 'butterscotch' rather than blue, as seen by Viking and Pathfinder.
cases.status_reason: Curiosity and Perseverance imagery confirm a butterscotch daytime sky with blue sunsets from dust forward-scattering.
cases.game_note: Sky colours of planets are not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Earth's magnetic field fails because the iron core stopped rotating.
cases.critique: Stopping the core would require removing ~1e35 erg of rotational energy, the Sun's output for ~100 s or five trillion one-megaton bombs - 'just plain old silly.'
cases.status_reason: The geodynamo is driven by convection in the liquid outer core; even 2023 seismic hints that the inner core's rotation relative to the mantle paused involve tiny differential motions, not a halt.
cases.game_note: Planetary interiors are not modelled.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Without the magnetic field, deadly cosmic rays and microwave beams from space strike Earth (one cuts the Golden Gate Bridge).
cases.critique: The magnetic field deflects some charged cosmic rays, but the atmosphere blocks most of them; a weakened field would not be deadly, and there are no natural space microwave beams to slice bridges.
cases.status_reason: Paleomagnetic records show past geomagnetic reversals/excursions (e.g. Laschamp, ~41 ka) caused no mass extinctions; the atmosphere provides ~10 m water-equivalent shielding.
cases.game_note: The sim computes surface dose including atmospheric shielding, so it would not make an exposed planet instantly deadly.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Krypton's red giant sun collapses and explodes as a supernova, tearing the planet apart.
cases.critique: A Sun-like red giant sheds its outer layers and leaves a white dwarf; it does not explode. (Comic canon also has the planet, not the star, exploding.)
cases.status_reason: Only stars above ~8 solar masses (red supergiants) undergo core-collapse supernovae; low-mass red giants end as planetary nebulae and white dwarfs.
cases.game_note: Stellar evolution and supernovae are not in the game (static stars, 7.4).

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Superman hovers motionless above the atmosphere, cape flapping, hearing a cry for help.
cases.critique: No sound in space - and his cape shouldn't flap since he isn't moving and there's no air.
cases.status_reason: No medium for sound or air drag above the atmosphere.
cases.game_note: No sound anywhere in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: A NASA engineer says you need only hit a baseball halfway to the Moon and the Moon's gravity takes over.
cases.critique: The Moon has ~1/80 Earth's mass, so at the halfway point Earth's pull is still ~80 times stronger; the balance point is about 90% of the way to the Moon.
cases.status_reason: Gravitational balance point ~346,000 km from Earth (~0.9 of the distance).
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: The engineer says jumping on a trampoline in space would make you go 'up and up and up'.
cases.critique: You can't really bounce on a trampoline in weightlessness: push off once and you just drift away, as from a wall, with nothing to bring you back.
cases.status_reason: Without a restoring force (gravity) there is no oscillating bounce.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Giant robots that crater the ground transform into ordinary-weight cars; the huge AllSpark cube shrinks to hand size.
cases.critique: Shrinking an object doesn't change its mass: a 10-20 ton robot folded into a car would be incredibly dense and heavy - 'Drive over a bridge and see what happens!'
cases.status_reason: Conservation of mass; density scales inversely with volume.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: An official says Earth's gravitational field at the North Pole scrambled Megatron's navigation.
cases.critique: The line clearly means the magnetic field; sci-fi constantly confuses gravity with magnetism.
cases.status_reason: Gravity is nearly uniform with latitude; it is the geomagnetic field that disturbs compasses near the poles.
cases.game_note: Not depicted; the game uses gravity and magnetism terms correctly (7.10, 4.4).

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Alien beam weapons blow planets into giant pieces in the opening montage.
cases.critique: It's really hard to blow up a planet: each piece must be given escape velocity (~11 km/s for Earth), an enormous gravitational binding energy.
cases.status_reason: Earth's gravitational binding energy is ~2e32 J, about a week of the Sun's total output.
cases.game_note: Planets are never destroyed in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: A crewman sucked out through a hull breach is implied to suffer boiling blood.
cases.critique: 'To the immediate point about blood boiling, it wouldn't happen' - the circulatory system keeps blood pressurized above vapor pressure.
cases.status_reason: Blood pressure keeps blood liquid in vacuum; only saliva/tears and tissue water (ebullism swelling) vaporize, per decompression-accident data.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Nero's mining drill bores a hole to Vulcan's core to drop red matter in.
cases.critique: Rock pressure would collapse the borehole and the plastic mantle would flow in: 'the pressure of the overlying rocks tends to collapse the hole.'
cases.status_reason: The deepest real borehole (Kola, 12 km) stalled because of heat and rock plasticity; a hole thousands of km deep is impossible.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: A drop of red matter turns Vulcan into a black hole that swallows the planet and endangers ships in orbit.
cases.critique: Making a black hole takes a lot of mass, infalling matter would blaze in X-rays, and once Vulcan collapsed 'the gravity felt by the orbiting ships didn't change!'
cases.status_reason: Outside a spherically symmetric mass, gravity depends only on enclosed mass (Birkhoff's theorem); a planet-mass black hole pulls no harder on orbiting ships.
cases.game_note: No black holes in the game (grep in 3).

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: From Delta Vega, Spock watches Vulcan's destruction looming huge in the sky.
cases.critique: For Vulcan to look that big, Delta Vega must be only a few hundred thousand km away at most - i.e. effectively a close moon of Vulcan (and he questions why an outpost would be there).
cases.status_reason: Angular size = diameter/distance; a planet subtending tens of degrees must be within roughly a few planetary radii to a few hundred thousand km.
cases.game_note: No sky views from planets are drawn.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: A supernova threatens to destroy the whole galaxy and Romulus.
cases.critique: Supernovae can only physically hurt planets within about 50 light-years; threatening the galaxy is absurd. Also 'as far as we know, yellow stars can't blow.'
cases.status_reason: The 'kill radius' estimate (~25-50 ly for ozone damage) still stands, and Sun-like single stars do not explode, but white dwarfs in binaries do (Type Ia), so 'yellow' systems are not fully immune.
cases.game_note: Supernovae are not in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Red-matter black hole is used to 'consume' the supernova and stop it.
cases.critique: A black hole wouldn't stop a supernova - core-collapse supernovae can already form black holes at their centers.
cases.status_reason: Core collapse itself forms neutron stars/black holes; the expanding ejecta would not be swallowed by a small central black hole.
cases.game_note: No black holes or supernovae in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Nero's ship and the Jellyfish are drawn into a black hole and the Enterprise escapes intact.
cases.critique: Tidal forces near a small black hole would rip the ship apart (spaghettification): 'The difference in gravity between your feet and head could be millions of times the Earth's gravity!'
cases.status_reason: Tidal acceleration ~2GM L/r^3 is enormous near a low-mass black hole's horizon.
cases.game_note: No black holes in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: The Enterprise ejects its warp core and is pushed away by the explosion's shock wave.
cases.critique: In vacuum there is no air to carry a shock wave; momentum transfer from expanding debris/radiation 'would be minimal'.
cases.status_reason: There is no air blast in space, but a very energetic explosion's debris and plasma could still impart momentum at close range, so the push is not strictly impossible.
cases.game_note: Battles are drawn as rings and bars with no blast waves.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Using a jetpack (MMU), Clooney and Bullock travel from Hubble to the ISS.
cases.critique: Hubble orbits ~110 m/s slower than the ISS and in an orbit 'tipped at wildly different angles'; the MMU can only deliver ~25 m/s, so the transfer is impossible.
cases.status_reason: Plane changes between 28.5 deg and 51.6 deg inclinations need km/s of delta-v; no crewed jetpack can do it.
cases.game_note: No near-Earth orbital manoeuvres in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Clooney, tethered and stopped relative to the ISS, drifts away and must let go to save Bullock.
cases.critique: Once they stopped they were in free fall with no net force; 'literally an ounce of force applied for a few seconds would've been enough' to pull him back.
cases.status_reason: Same point as Tyson; with zero relative velocity there is no tension pulling him away (only minor tidal/rotational effects).
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Bullock uses a fire extinguisher as a thruster to reach Tiangong.
cases.critique: Probably impossible: thrusting with an extinguisher not aligned through her center of mass would send her tumbling; and Tiangong's orbit is inclined ~10 deg from the ISS so a Soyuz couldn't easily match it either.
cases.status_reason: Off-axis thrust produces torque; plane changes are expensive in delta-v.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Shuttle crew killed by debris are shown frozen almost immediately.
cases.critique: Freezing bodies in vacuum would take hours, since heat leaves only by radiation (and slow evaporation).
cases.status_reason: Radiative cooling of a human-mass body takes many hours; vacuum is an insulator.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Debris from a destroyed satellite returns every ~90 minutes to hit Hubble, the shuttle and the ISS.
cases.critique: Debris stays in roughly its parent's orbit, so it could only hit Hubble and ISS if satellite orbits intersected theirs, which operators avoid; debris would not sweep all altitudes and inclinations together.
cases.status_reason: Fragment clouds spread along the parent orbit (seen after the 2007 Fengyun-1C and 2021 Kosmos-1408 ASAT tests) rather than covering all altitudes.
cases.game_note: No orbital debris in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Miller's planet orbits Gargantua so close that one hour there equals seven years on Earth (~60,000x time dilation).
cases.critique: Such dilation requires skimming the horizon, but 'the minimum stable orbit around a black hole must be at least three times the size of the black hole itself,' so the planet would fall in.
cases.status_reason: Plait retracted it two days later: for a near-maximally spinning Kerr black hole (as Kip Thorne specified) stable orbits exist close enough for that dilation; he wrote the film's time dilation 'was in fact accurate.' (source of retraction: https://www.syfy.com/syfy-wire/follow-interstellar-mea-culpa)
cases.game_note: No black holes in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Giant mountain-high waves roll across the shallow seas of Miller's planet.
cases.critique: Kept after his mea culpa: he still objects to the giant 'tidal waves', arguing such a planet's tides and shallow seas could not produce them.
cases.status_reason: A perfectly locked planet would have static tides, but Thorne's explanation (a slight rocking libration producing periodic tidal bores) is physically plausible; the critique holds only for an exactly locked orbit.
cases.game_note: Tides are not modelled (tidal locking is a display label only, 7.9).

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Planets around Gargantua are lit and warmed although there is no star nearby; the accretion disk looks calm and dim.
cases.critique: 'Where do the planets get heat and light?' The disk isn't bright enough to light and heat the planets; a real disk would be extremely hot and fast-moving, and planets would be pelted by infalling matter.
cases.status_reason: Thorne deliberately chose an unusually cold, quiescent disk, which is then too dim to warm planets as Plait says; but a brighter disk would irradiate them with X-rays, so the scenario is internally strained rather than simply wrong.
cases.game_note: No black-hole-lit planets; habitability is tied to real stars.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: The Enterprise whooshes audibly past the camera in space.
cases.critique: 'Well, it's Trek. That means we hear sounds in space' - sound needs a medium; even a nebula's gas could not carry sound as we know it, and computer-added-sound retcons don't explain what outside viewers hear.
cases.status_reason: No acoustic propagation in vacuum; interstellar gas densities (~1 atom/cm^3) cannot carry audible sound.
cases.game_note: No sound in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: At warp 4.5 the ship reaches Neptune and back in six minutes, yet the Klingon homeworld is 'four days' away.
cases.critique: Six minutes to Neptune and back is ~80c; four days at 80c is under one light-year - closer than the nearest star, Proxima Centauri (~20 days' travel at that speed).
cases.status_reason: Proxima Centauri at 4.24 ly remains the nearest star; simple distance/speed arithmetic.
cases.game_note: Star distances are real CNS5 positions, so travel-time arithmetic is honest.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Stars stream rapidly past the windows during warp.
cases.critique: If the nearest star takes ~20 days to reach, roughly one star should flash by every ~20 days on average; the streaks can't be dust because they resolve into stars when the ship drops out of warp.
cases.status_reason: Mean interstellar spacing (~5 ly locally) means stars pass very rarely even at 80c.
cases.game_note: Nothing is rendered from a moving ship's viewpoint (6.3).

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: A comet cruises through an asteroid belt crowded with hundreds of visible rocks and smashes into two of them.
cases.critique: Even in the thickest part of the belt, asteroids are typically millions of miles apart; a comet hitting even one is unlikely, two essentially impossible.
cases.status_reason: Spacecraft (Pioneer, Galileo, Dawn, Lucy) cross the belt without special avoidance; mean separations are ~1e6 km.
cases.game_note: No asteroid fields are drawn.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author

cases.critique: Fragments knocked onto the new orbit stay on that orbit and travel with the main body; they would not arrive days ahead.

cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author

cases.status_reason: Megawatt-class airborne lasers (the cancelled YAL-1 program) deliver far too little energy to vaporize a mountain-sized body.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: An iron asteroid ~10x5x3 km at 50,000 mph is said to hit with the force of 30 atomic bombs.
cases.critique: An iron body that size at that speed would release vastly more energy than 30 atomic bombs - the line 'made me laugh out loud'.
cases.status_reason: KE ~ 0.5 x 1.2e15 kg x (22 km/s)^2 ~ 3e23 J, about 70 million megatons.
cases.game_note: Like the film's underestimate, the game ignores that each 0.9c fleet carries ~4e12 Mt of kinetic energy (5.2).

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Nineteen minutes before impact, the incoming asteroid is shown passing over the Moon.
cases.critique: The Moon is ~250,000 miles away, five hours at 50,000 mph; 19 minutes out the rock would be only ~17,000 miles away, closer than geosynchronous satellites.
cases.status_reason: Simple distance/speed arithmetic.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
cases.depiction: Two nuclear missiles blow up the iron asteroid.
cases.critique: The asteroid is roughly the volume of Mt. Everest and solid iron; two atomic bombs 'would not do a whole lot of damage' and certainly wouldn't vaporize it.
cases.status_reason: Two small fission bombs indeed could not vaporize it, but standoff-burst studies (e.g. the 2024 Sandia Z-machine X-ray ablation experiment in Nature Physics) show nuclear X-ray pulses can usefully deflect km-scale bodies, so nukes are not useless if the goal is deflection.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History

cases.status_reason: General relativity predicts spaghettification for stellar-mass holes and extreme time dilation near the horizon; EHT images (2019, 2022) show luminous accretion flows, not caverns.
cases.game_note: No black holes in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
cases.depiction: Ellie says if one in a million stars has planets, one in a million of those has life, and one in a million of those intelligent life, there would be millions of civilizations.

cases.status_reason: The arithmetic is correct; moreover Kepler/TESS results show most stars host planets, so the movie's 'one in a million have planets' factor is also far too pessimistic.
cases.game_note: Drake-style odds imply rare intelligence, yet the game places 11 native civilisations among 73 real nearby systems, including an information-age one at Barnard's Star.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
cases.depiction: Hours on Miller's planet near the black hole Gargantua equal years on Earth.
cases.critique: Strong gravity really slows time ('is real, by the way'); an extreme case is plausible because 'they made it clear this is a planet orbiting a black hole.'
cases.status_reason: Gravitational time dilation is measured daily (GPS) and the ~60,000x factor is attainable near a rapidly spinning supermassive black hole (Thorne 2014).
cases.game_note: Time dilation is real and should matter; the game never displays proper (ship) time, only Earth-frame years.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
cases.depiction: The crew travels to another galaxy through a wormhole near Saturn.
cases.critique: Wormhole math and physics are sound, 'but we don't know how to make one, and even if we did make one, the equations show that they're unstable.'

cases.game_note: The game has no wormholes or other FTL travel; all ships are sub-light.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
cases.depiction: The Moon is revealed to be a hollow artificial megastructure knocked from its orbit toward Earth.
cases.critique: Said Moonfall dethroned Armageddon as the biggest violator of physical laws, mocking the hollow Moon containing a giant built structure.
cases.status_reason: Apollo seismometers, the Moon's moment of inertia (0.393) and GRAIL gravity mapping show a solid, differentiated body with a small dense core - not hollow.
cases.game_note: Moon interiors are not depicted.

cases.depiction: Debris from a destroyed satellite sweeps around Earth and strikes the shuttle, Hubble and ISS.
cases.critique: Tweet: 'Nearly all satellites orbit Earth west to east yet all satellite debris portrayed orbited east to west' - debris should share the prograde motion of its parent satellites.
cases.status_reason: Almost all satellites are launched prograde to use Earth's rotation; fragments keep roughly their parent's orbit, so retrograde debris streams are implausible.
cases.game_note: No orbital debris in the game.

cases.depiction: Sandra Bullock's hair stays neatly in place during otherwise convincing weightless scenes.
cases.critique: Tweet: 'Why Bullock's hair, in otherwise convincing zero-G scenes, did not float freely on her head.'
cases.status_reason: In free fall hair has no weight to pull it down and drifts freely, as ISS footage shows.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.status_reason: Once the pair's motion relative to the station has stopped there is no net force pulling Clooney away; a gentle tug would bring him back (residual rotation could add only a small tension).
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History

cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History

cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
cases.depiction: BB-8, a rolling spherical droid, travels smoothly across desert sand.
cases.critique: Tweet: 'BB-8, a smooth rolling metal spherical ball, would have skidded uncontrollably on sand.'
cases.status_reason: A smooth ball-drive has poor traction on loose sand, but the real BB-8 prop (and Sphero toy) roll on sand using an internal drive with grippy surface; the problem is traction design, not impossibility.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
cases.depiction: TIE fighters scream audibly in space battles.
cases.critique: Tweet: 'the TIE fighters made exactly the same sound in the vacuum of space as in planetary atmospheres.'
cases.status_reason: Sound requires a medium; there is no propagation through vacuum.
cases.game_note: No sound in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
cases.depiction: Han Solo repeats the boast that the Millennium Falcon made the Kessel Run in under 12 parsecs.
cases.critique: Tweets: 'repeats the Millennium Falcon boast of completing the Kessel Run in under 12 parsecs' - 'A Parsec is ... a unit of distance ... equal to 3.26 Light Years. Neither has anything to do with time.'
cases.status_reason: A parsec is indeed a distance (3.26 ly), but the franchise later (Solo, 2018) framed the boast as a shorter route, so a distance claim is not physically absurd.
cases.game_note: The game uses light-years consistently as distance and derives times from them (1 ly = 1 yr of light delay).

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
cases.depiction: Starkiller Base drains its star's energy into the planet to power a superweapon.
cases.critique: Tweet: 'if you were to suck all of a star's energy into your planet, your planet would vaporize.'
cases.status_reason: A star's output (~1e26 W for a Sun-like star, total ~1e44 J) vastly exceeds the ~1e32 J gravitational binding energy of an Earth-like planet.
cases.game_note: The game also harvests star output without consequence: Sol's swarm reaches ~99% coverage with no effect on Earth and stores up to 10 years of output with no stated medium.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
cases.depiction: Thor's hammer Mjolnir, said in Marvel lore to be forged in the heart of a dying star, is wielded one-handed.
cases.critique: Tweet: 'If Thor's hammer is made of neutron-star matter, implied by legend, then it weighs as much as a herd of 300-billion elephants.'
cases.status_reason: The density arithmetic (~1e15 kg for a hammer-sized volume of ~4e17 kg/m^3 matter) is right, but canon makes Mjolnir of fictional Uru, and neutron-degenerate matter cannot stay compressed outside a neutron star anyway.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
cases.depiction: Superman views the location of his home planet Krypton; the comic places Krypton around a real star chosen by Tyson.
cases.critique: Tyson selected the red dwarf LHS 2520 in Corvus, stated as 27.1 light-years away, as Krypton's sun - a red star 'cooler and smaller than our sun', consistent with the red-sun Superman lore.
cases.status_reason: Gaia parallax (81.57 mas) puts LHS 2520 at ~40 light-years, not 27.1.
cases.game_note: The game's star catalogue is CNS5 (Gaia-era astrometry), so it would use the corrected ~40 ly distance.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
cases.depiction: Starships jump from rest to large fractions of light speed in seconds with crew unharmed; 'inertial dampers' cancel acceleration
cases.critique: Humans tolerate only ~3 g; at that limit it would take ~2.5 months to reach half light speed, and sudden acceleration would turn the crew into 'chunky salsa'; inertial dampers amount to suspending Newton's laws and are never explained
cases.status_reason: Basic Newtonian mechanics and human g-tolerance; no known mechanism shields bodies from inertial forces (equivalence principle).
cases.game_note: G accelerates crewed ships instantly to 0.95c (1.2) and both editions reverse fleets instantly on redirect (4.7); only S uses a survivable 1g.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
cases.depiction: Crews travel near light speed on long missions yet stay in sync with Starfleet Command and home time
cases.critique: Special-relativistic time dilation means a 10-year crew mission near light speed could correspond to ~25,000 years at home; commanders back home would have retired; a quarter-light-speed cap keeps clocks synchronized but makes ships far too slow
cases.status_reason: Time dilation is experimentally confirmed (muon lifetimes, GPS, atomic clocks on aircraft).
cases.game_note: Like Star Trek, the game never shows crew/colonist proper time; all 'X years' are Earth-frame and travellers do not age in transit.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
cases.depiction: Warp drive lets ships travel faster than light by warping space
cases.critique: GR permits space to expand behind and contract ahead of a ship, but it needs exotic negative-energy matter never observed and a gravitational field whose creation would require more energy than the Sun emits over its whole lifetime
cases.status_reason: The negative-energy requirement still holds (all warp metrics violate the energy conditions, Santiago-Schuster-Visser 2022), but energy estimates have dropped a lot since 1995 (Van Den Broeck 1999; White 2011; Bobrick & Martire 2021), so the 'Sun's lifetime output' figure is no longer the consensus number.
cases.game_note: No warp drive in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
cases.work: Star Trek (franchise, incl. Deep Space Nine)
cases.depiction: Stable traversable wormholes used as travel routes (e.g., the Bajoran wormhole)
cases.critique: Holding a wormhole open would need large, long-lasting amounts of negative energy; negative energy has only been seen briefly and in tiny amounts (Casimir effect), so whether it is possible is unknown
cases.status_reason: Still the standard view (Morris-Thorne; quantum inequalities limit negative energy); no macroscopic exotic matter has been found.
cases.game_note: No wormholes in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
cases.depiction: Holodeck creates solid, touchable objects and people from projected light
cases.critique: Projecting light images is consistent with physics and limited mostly by computing, but 'there's no way to make an image of light solid'
cases.status_reason: Photons don't form rigid bound structures at everyday intensities; lab 'molecules of light' (2013 Rydberg experiments) are microscopic and transient.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
cases.depiction: Transporter dematerializes a person and sends their actual atoms elsewhere
cases.critique: Breaking the electromagnetic bonds of an adult-mass body would take over 1,000 times the world's annual energy output; moving the actual atoms as shown is not possible; at best you could send information and rebuild, vaporizing the original
cases.status_reason: The energy scale argument (mc^2 and binding energies) is sound; quantum teleportation moves states, not matter.
cases.game_note: No teleporters; matter moves only by ship (except the refugee leak 2.8i).

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
cases.depiction: Transporter scans every atom of a person precisely enough to rebuild them
cases.critique: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle makes it impossible to resolve atoms and their energy states accurately enough to recreate a human pattern; resolving atom-sized detail at 40,000 km range would need X/gamma-ray optics with a 'lens' ~50,000 km across
cases.status_reason: Reinforced by the no-cloning theorem; quantum teleportation (demonstrated since 1997) needs pre-shared entanglement and destroys the original state, unlike the show's scanner.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
cases.depiction: Phaser beams are visible as bright streaks crossing empty space
cases.critique: A laser beam in a vacuum is invisible except where it hits dust or a target; it is visible 'only at the point of impact'
cases.status_reason: Light is only seen when scattered into the eye; interplanetary space has almost nothing to scatter it.
cases.game_note: The map draws light-speed signals as visible moving dots, though a beam not aimed at the observer is invisible; the legend labels it a display choice.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
cases.depiction: Crew hears explosions and ship flybys outside the ship in space
cases.critique: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum ('In space, no one can hear you scream'), yet the crew hears external explosions
cases.status_reason: Sound needs a medium; interstellar gas is far too thin to carry audible sound.
cases.game_note: No sound in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); then chair of physics, Case Western Reserve University
cases.depiction: An episode gives an object's temperature as -293 degrees C
cases.critique: Blooper: absolute zero is -273 C, so -293 C is impossible
cases.status_reason: Absolute zero is the lower bound on the Kelvin/Celsius scale; lab 'negative absolute temperatures' (2013) are hotter than any positive temperature, not colder.
cases.game_note: Not depicted; game temperatures are physically bounded equilibrium values.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); Ambrose Swasey Professor of Physics, Case Western Reserve University at time of writing
cases.depiction: The alien Mother Ship, about 1/4 the Moon's mass, parks in geostationary orbit while the attack goes ahead
cases.critique: At ~22,500 miles (about 1/10 the lunar distance) its gravitational pull on Earth would be ~25 times the Moon's; the resulting tides would flood coastal cities and tidal stress would trigger earthquakes and eruptions before a shot was fired; it would also perturb Earth's motion and could brake Earth's rotation
cases.status_reason: Inverse-square gravity; tidal forces scale as M/r^3, so the tidal effect would actually be ~250x lunar, which makes the point stronger.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); Ambrose Swasey Professor of Physics, Case Western Reserve University at time of writing
cases.depiction: 15-mile-wide alien saucers hover silently a few thousand feet above cities
cases.critique: A craft that size (~100 billion tons) hovering that low must push on the air below with ~450 psi (~30 atm), roughly 30 tons per square foot; buildings collapse at ~5 atm overpressure, so the saucers would flatten cities just by hovering, whatever their lift mechanism
cases.status_reason: Momentum conservation: any hovering craft must transfer its weight to the air below; at altitude much less than its width, the pressure isn't spread out.
cases.game_note: No hovering craft in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); Ambrose Swasey Professor of Physics, Case Western Reserve University at time of writing
cases.depiction: Downed alien city-destroyers crash to Earth and humanity celebrates victory
cases.critique: A single saucer falling from ~1 mile would release ~10,000 Hiroshima bombs' worth of energy, comparable to a dinosaur-killing impact; accelerating one to 3 mi/s in a minute would need ~5x10^19 W, ~300 times the solar power reaching Earth
cases.status_reason: Simple mgh with his assumed mass gives ~1.6e18 J (~25,000 Hiroshimas), consistent with his order of magnitude.
cases.game_note: Like the film's victory party ignoring crash energy, the game ignores the planet-killing kinetic energy of its own fleets (5.2).

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); Ambrose Swasey Professor of Physics, Case Western Reserve University at time of writing
cases.depiction: The quarter-Moon-mass Mother Ship decelerates into Earth orbit
cases.critique: Slowing an object that massive into orbit within an hour would require engines radiating almost 10 times the Sun's entire luminosity, from only 22,500 miles away, toasting Earth
cases.status_reason: Kinetic-energy bookkeeping (½mv^2 over a short time) gives power of order the solar luminosity; no new physics changes this.
cases.game_note: Braking a huge mass quickly needs enormous power; G brakes 0.95c ships instantly and S brakes magsails at an impossible 1g.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); Ambrose Swasey Professor of Physics, Case Western Reserve University at time of writing
cases.depiction: UFOs at a secret air base fly at great speed and make instant 90-degree turns; human test pilots fly them
cases.critique: A craft at ~twice the speed of sound turning 90 degrees in 0.1 s feels ~700 g; neither the pilots nor the craft's structure could survive that, so real alien craft would not move that way
cases.status_reason: a = Δv/Δt ≈ 700 m/s / 0.1 s ≈ 7,000 m/s² ≈ 700 g; Newton's second law still holds.
cases.game_note: Fleets reverse course instantly on redirect and cargo turns at 0.95c at waypoints with no delta-v booked, the same impossible-turn flaw.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (Princeton 1965); Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics Emeritus, Caltech; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017; science advisor and executive producer of Interstellar
cases.depiction: Mann's planet has frozen clouds and ice structures that hold up large overhangs and the crew walk on them
cases.critique: Thorne named this the film's most troubling physics error: ice is not strong enough to support the frozen-cloud structures shown, though he called it minor
cases.status_reason: Ice's compressive and tensile strength (~1-10 MPa) can't support km-scale floating overhangs in Earth-like gravity.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (Princeton 1965); Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics Emeritus, Caltech; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017; science advisor and executive producer of Interstellar
cases.depiction: Miller's planet orbits extremely close to Gargantua, where 1 hour equals ~7 Earth years, and isn't torn apart
cases.critique: He first thought this was impossible, then calculated it works only if Gargantua spins extremely fast (very close to maximal) and is very massive (>=100 million solar masses), allowing a stable close orbit with huge time dilation and tolerable tides
cases.status_reason: Kerr geometry allows it in principle, but the spin needed (within ~1e-14 of maximal) is far above the ~0.998 'Thorne limit' that accretion and radiation should cap real black holes at.
cases.game_note: No black holes in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (Princeton 1965); Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics Emeritus, Caltech; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017; science advisor and executive producer of Interstellar
cases.depiction: Huge mountain-height waves sweep Miller's planet about once an hour
cases.critique: Explained speculatively: the tidally locked planet rocks back and forth in Gargantua's tidal field, driving giant tides; the waves look like non-breaking solitons, perhaps like tidal bores; the rocking period would also need to be about one hour
cases.status_reason: A forced libration can drive tides in principle, but a planet in a stable tidally locked orbit should damp the rocking, and later analyses (e.g., arXiv:1503.08305) find no worked-out model for 1-km waves.
cases.game_note: Tides are not modelled.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (Princeton 1965); Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics Emeritus, Caltech; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017; science advisor and executive producer of Interstellar
cases.depiction: Astronauts and a planet sit near Gargantua's accretion disk without being irradiated
cases.critique: Gargantua's disk is 'anemic': cool, no longer fed by inflowing gas, so it lacks the X-rays and gamma rays a typical quasar-like disk would emit and that would kill the humans
cases.status_reason: Low-luminosity disks exist (Sgr A* is very faint, as EHT 2022 confirmed), but a disk shining as brightly in visible light as shown would be fairly hot and still emit UV/X-rays.
cases.game_note: No black holes or accretion disks in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (Princeton 1965); Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics Emeritus, Caltech; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017; science advisor and executive producer of Interstellar
cases.depiction: A wormhole near Saturn makes interstellar travel possible (Thorne also dropped warp drive and FTL from early drafts)
cases.critique: The laws of physics forbid FTL travel and 'very probably forbid warp drives and traversable wormholes', though this isn't fully proven; the wormhole is placed in the film's speculative category
cases.status_reason: Still the mainstream view: traversable wormholes need exotic matter; recent constructions (Maldacena-Milekhin 2018, the 2022 'wormhole-on-a-chip' simulation) are tiny, need special conditions, or aren't usable for travel.
cases.game_note: The game obeys this: no FTL, warp or wormholes.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (Princeton 1965); Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics Emeritus, Caltech; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017; co-author with DNEG VFX team
cases.depiction: Gargantua's accretion disk is shown symmetric in colour and brightness
cases.critique: A real disk with material moving at ~0.55c would be Doppler-shifted and beamed: blue and very bright on the approaching side, red and dim on the receding side (frequency factors ~1.5 and ~0.4 with ~20% gravitational redshift); the filmmakers deliberately left this out to avoid confusing audiences
cases.status_reason: Confirmed by Event Horizon Telescope images of M87* (2019) and Sgr A* (2022), which show strong brightness asymmetry from relativistic beaming.
cases.game_note: No black holes; Doppler/beaming are consistently not shown since all views are rest-frame maps (6.3).

cases.credentials: PhD physics (Princeton 1965); Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics Emeritus, Caltech; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017; co-author with DNEG VFX team
cases.depiction: Gargantua's on-screen image has a nearly circular shadow and centred disk
cases.critique: The story's huge time losses need a near-maximally spinning hole (a/M≈1), whose shadow is flattened on one side with an off-centre disk; for visual clarity the filmmakers rendered it with spin a/M=0.6, inconsistent with the plot
cases.status_reason: Standard Kerr ray-tracing result; EHT work confirms the spin-dependent shadow shapes such codes predict.
cases.game_note: No black holes in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD planetary physics (UCLA); NASA JPL research scientist on the Cassini mission; science advisor to Battlestar Galactica, Eureka, Gravity
cases.depiction: Galactica (over a km long) jumps into New Caprica's atmosphere, falls in a 'belly flop', launches Vipers and jumps out intact (episode 'Exodus, Part 2')
cases.critique: A ship that size plunging into an atmosphere would 'do what Columbia did' and break up; he let the scene stand for its 'coolness factor'
cases.status_reason: Aerodynamic and thermal loads on a huge non-aerodynamic hull are severe, but since the ship arrives by FTL jump with little orbital velocity, it wouldn't get Columbia-style reentry heating, so breakup isn't certain.
cases.game_note: No atmospheric entry in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD planetary physics (UCLA); NASA JPL research scientist on the Cassini mission; science advisor to Battlestar Galactica
cases.depiction: Galactica rams the Cylon Colony at speed after jumping in about 100 m away (series finale 'Daybreak')
cases.critique: With KE = ½mv², a ship that close couldn't build much speed even at 'flank speed' over ~100 m, so the ram couldn't deliver the energy implied
cases.status_reason: Basic kinematics: v = √(2ad) is small for any survivable acceleration over 100 m.
cases.game_note: Kinetic energy is never applied as a weapon or hazard in the game, although its fleets carry relativistic KE (5.2).

cases.credentials: PhD planetary physics (UCLA); NASA JPL research scientist on the Cassini mission; science advisor to Battlestar Galactica
cases.depiction: Ships have uniform artificial gravity from deck-plate generators; 'zero-g' is rarely shown
cases.critique: FTL and artificial gravity have no known physics; a line of gravity generators would make a cylindrical field falling off as 1/r (not 1/r²), so hallway floors would effectively bow; spin gravity on a ring ship would need fast rotation and has its own problems; zero-g is mostly avoided for production reasons
cases.status_reason: Gauss's-law geometry gives 1/r for line sources; no mechanism for artificial gravity other than acceleration/rotation is known.
cases.game_note: Ship interiors and artificial gravity are not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD planetary physics (UCLA); NASA JPL research scientist on the Cassini mission; science advisor to Battlestar Galactica
cases.depiction: Humanoid Cylons are physically indistinguishable from humans, yet Baltar builds a 'Cylon detector'
cases.critique: The Cylons' 'silica pathways' mean SiO2 (glass), which is inert, so a Cylon would show an anomalously high silica level in a mass spectrometer, which makes a detector plausible
cases.status_reason: Mass spectrometry readily measures elemental silicon abundance; human tissue has very little silicon.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD geophysics and space physics (UCLA); 15 years at NASA JPL (Cassini); science advisor to Gravity

cases.critique: From Hubble's orbit you can't reach the ISS on one spacewalk's oxygen; the trip is at least about LA-to-Mexico-border distance; he suggested a telescope in a closer orbit, but the production kept Hubble for drama
cases.status_reason: Hubble (~540 km, 28.5°) and ISS (~420 km, 51.6°) are in different orbital planes; the plane change alone needs km/s of delta-v, far beyond an MMU.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD geophysics and space physics (UCLA); 15 years at NASA JPL (Cassini); science advisor to Gravity
cases.depiction: A debris cascade from a destroyed satellite shreds spacecraft and keeps returning
cases.critique: The premise rests on the Kessler Syndrome; the scale of damage is plausible 'for the level of scientific veracity needed to tell this story'
cases.status_reason: Kessler cascades are a real risk (cf. the 2021 Russian ASAT test debris), but they develop over years, and debris from one breakup wouldn't hit objects in very different orbits within hours.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD geophysics and space physics (UCLA); 15 years at NASA JPL (Cassini); science advisor to Gravity
cases.depiction: The shuttle is hit by debris and sent spinning rapidly with Dr. Stone attached to the arm
cases.critique: Spin rate depends on impactor speed and mass; he isn't sure the film's spin is realistic, and the wing would more likely be sheared off than the orbiter sent spinning
cases.status_reason: Hypervelocity (~km/s) impacts of small debris punch through or shear structures; they transfer little angular momentum to a 100-tonne orbiter.
cases.game_note: Hypervelocity impacts punch through structures; S folds dust into average dose and ignores discrete grain impacts at 0.95c (9.4), and G has no hazard at all.

cases.credentials: PhD geophysics and space physics (UCLA); 15 years at NASA JPL (Cassini); science advisor to Gravity
cases.depiction: Stone is spinning on the end of the shuttle's robotic arm and Kowalski tells her to detach so he can rescue her
cases.critique: The arm is far more massive than the astronaut on it, so it's much more realistic to find enough delta-v to stop Stone alone; on release her velocity is the arm's centre-of-mass motion plus the rotational component, which could send her 'a pretty good kick' back toward Kowalski and Earth
cases.status_reason: Momentum and rigid-body kinematics: a released body keeps its tangential velocity, and its small mass makes it easier to arrest than the arm-plus-shuttle.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS (Centre de Physique Théorique / Laboratoire d'Astrophysique de Marseille); made the first computed image of a black hole with an accretion disk (1979)
cases.depiction: Gargantua is taken to spin within ~1e-10 (or less) of the maximal Kerr value to allow Miller's planet's orbit and the 1 hour = 7 years dilation
cases.critique: Theoretically possible but 'by no ways realistic': prograde matter is hard to accrete while retrograde matter falls in easily and slows the spin, so real holes should top out near 0.998 J_max
cases.status_reason: The Thorne (1974) spin limit of ~0.998 still holds; spin measurements by X-ray reflection and LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA give high spins but none near 1 - 1e-10.
cases.game_note: No black holes in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS, Marseille; pioneer of black-hole imaging (1979)
cases.depiction: The planets around Gargantua are lit and warmed with no star nearby, and astronauts aren't harmed by the accretion disk
cases.critique: A normal accretion disk is millions of degrees and would fry the astronauts as they leave the wormhole (and Cooper later when he falls in); Thorne's 'anemic' sun-temperature disk would be optically thin, so Luminet doubts it could give a planet Sun-like light and heat
cases.status_reason: Radiatively inefficient, low-accretion flows (like Sgr A*'s, measured by EHT/GRAVITY) are very dim and couldn't warm a habitable planet.
cases.game_note: No black holes in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS, Marseille; pioneer of black-hole imaging (1979)
cases.depiction: Gargantua's accretion disk is shown uniformly bright, billed as the most realistic black-hole image ever made
cases.critique: Basic effects are missing: a thin disk's emission peaks in the hot inner regions, and gravitational (Einstein) redshift plus Doppler shifts and beaming make the apparent brightness strongly non-uniform and asymmetric; his own 1979 simulation already included these
cases.status_reason: Confirmed by EHT images of M87* (2019) and Sgr A* (2022), which show the predicted beaming asymmetry.
cases.game_note: No black holes in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS, Marseille; researcher on tidal disruption of stars by black holes
cases.depiction: Miller's planet orbits just outside Gargantua's horizon without being torn apart
cases.critique: Bloggers claimed it should be shredded, but the Roche limit for a 1e8-solar-mass hole and a ~1 g/cm³ planet (~1e13 cm) is about the gravitational radius, so the planet feels large tides but survives; the film is 'marginally correct'
cases.status_reason: Roche limit scales as (M/ρ)^(1/3) while horizon radius scales as M, so very massive holes have Roche limits near or inside the horizon, consistent with observed tidal disruption events around lower-mass SMBHs.
cases.game_note: No black holes in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS, Marseille
cases.depiction: Kilometre-high waves sweep Miller's planet about once an hour
cases.critique: He suspects an inconsistency: a tidal 'wave' is really a fixed bulge the planet rotates through, but with tides this strong the planet should tidally lock almost instantly (he estimates ~1 ms), after which the water stays put pointing at the hole, so no periodic waves
cases.status_reason: The tidal-locking argument is sound, but a ~1 ms locking time is implausibly short as an estimate, and Thorne's alternative (forced libration of a locked planet) isn't ruled out by it.
cases.game_note: The game flags close-in planets as tidally locked (7.9), though without climate consequences.

cases.status_reason: The Penrose physics is right (29% extractable for a=1), but the film and Thorne's book describe the boost as a slingshot plus Newton's-third-law ejection, not a true negative-energy-orbit Penrose process.
cases.game_note: No black holes in the game.

cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.critique: Except for the correct spherical look on approach, most of Thorne's wormhole-crossing calculations were dropped as too confusing; a traversable wormhole is 'very improbable' and, if one existed, crossing it 'would not at all look like it is shown in the movie'; it's also unclear that normal-matter humans could safely cross the negative-energy region
cases.status_reason: Ray-traced views (James et al. 2015, Am. J. Phys.) differ from the film's tunnel sequence, and no macroscopic traversable wormhole solution with ordinary matter is known.
cases.game_note: No wormholes in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS, Marseille
cases.depiction: Cooper falls into Gargantua, survives, and reaches a tesseract from which he can affect the past
cases.critique: In a Schwarzschild hole tidal forces at the centre would destroy him, but Gargantua's high spin gives an avoidable ring singularity, so idealized Kerr geometry lets him pass through as through a wormhole; black-hole physics gives 'no firm answers' on travel to the past
cases.status_reason: The ideal Kerr interior allows this, but in realistic perturbed holes the inner (Cauchy) horizon is unstable (mass inflation, Poisson-Israel 1990; Dafermos-Luk 2017), so the passage through to other regions likely doesn't survive.
cases.game_note: No black holes in the game.

cases.status_reason: Still true in 2026: no accepted theory of quantum gravity decides whether closed timelike curves are allowed (Hawking's chronology protection conjecture is unproven).
cases.game_note: No time travel in the game.

cases.status_reason: The paradox objection is widely held, but GR has closed-timelike-curve solutions and self-consistent (Novikov) or branching (Deutsch) models avoid paradoxes; the question remains open.
cases.game_note: No time travel in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (UC Berkeley 1972); Henry Semat Professor of Theoretical Physics, City College of New York; co-founder of string field theory

cases.game_note: No teleportation in the game.

cases.status_reason: Warp metrics still need negative energy and huge energy budgets (Santiago-Schuster-Visser 2022), far beyond any lab.

cases.critique: Based on Project Orion with antimatter charges instead of nuclear warheads; calculations suggest such a ship could reach about 0.5-0.8 c
cases.status_reason: Antimatter has the right energy density in principle, but pusher-plate pulse drives are limited to a few % of c by plate ablation and heat, and the tonnes of antimatter needed are ~1e15x current production (CERN makes nanograms).
cases.game_note: The game's antimatter braking assumes Forward's optimistic 1e-4 production efficiency (today ~1e-9), so antimatter supply is far cheaper than physics now allows.

cases.credentials: PhD geophysics and space physics (UCLA); NASA JPL research scientist (Cassini); science advisor to Virtuality
cases.depiction: The crew make a 10-year round trip to Epsilon Eridani (~10.5 light-years away)
cases.critique: The target was chosen because, at ~0.9 c and taking relativistic time dilation/length contraction into account, it is reachable within a ten-year round trip of crew time
cases.status_reason: 21 ly at 0.9 c is ~23 Earth years but ~10 years of proper time (γ ≈ 2.3), ignoring acceleration phases; Epsilon Eridani's distance (10.5 ly) is confirmed by Gaia.
cases.game_note: The work uses proper time correctly; the game never shows proper time (only Earth-frame years), and Epsilon Eridani is not even on its +/-2 ly map.

cases.credentials: PhD high-energy physics (Manchester 1998); Professor of Particle Physics, University of Manchester; science advisor to Sunshine
cases.depiction: The Sun is dying because a Q-ball (exotic supersymmetric particle) has lodged in it; a Moon-mass bomb was planned to reignite it
cases.critique: In reality the Sun is not dense enough to stop a Q-ball, so the backstory is creative licence; he had the bomb scaled down from the mass of the Moon to the size of Manhattan, and said several inaccuracies were allowed to serve the plot
cases.status_reason: Q-balls are still hypothetical (no detection at LHC or in dark-matter searches), and a weakly interacting relativistic particle would pass through solar plasma; any bomb is negligible next to the Sun's ~4e26 W output.
cases.game_note: No exotic stellar physics in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); Ambrose Swasey Professor of Physics, Case Western Reserve University at time of writing
cases.depiction: The Millennium Falcon banks like an aircraft when it turns in space
cases.critique: Planes bank because they turn using air pressure on their wings; in space wings play no part in propulsion, so there's no reason to bank. It's done because 'it looks good'
cases.status_reason: Spacecraft change direction by thrust vectoring and attitude control; no aerodynamic lift exists in vacuum.
cases.game_note: Ship attitude and banking are never drawn (ships are map markers).

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); Ambrose Swasey Professor of Physics, Case Western Reserve University at time of writing
