cases.critique: There's no air in space, so banking and the nacelle movement serve no physical purpose; the answer to 'why?' is simply 'It looks good'
cases.status_reason: Without an atmosphere, attitude changes give no lift; nacelle geometry has no known physical role in any real warp metric.
cases.game_note: Ship attitude is never drawn.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (MIT 1982); Ambrose Swasey Professor of Physics, Case Western Reserve University at time of writing
cases.depiction: Rotating spacecraft and stations create artificial gravity by spin
cases.critique: Praised as a correct depiction: spinning a large structure throws occupants against the outer wall, which is exactly how long flights will produce artificial gravity; by contrast, small, rapidly spinning TV flying saucers would pin their crew to the perimeter and gain nothing from saucer aerodynamics in vacuum
cases.status_reason: Centripetal acceleration ω²r is the only practical artificial-gravity method known; studies favour large radii (>~100 m) to limit Coriolis effects, as 2001's large wheel station does.
cases.game_note: Spin is the only practical artificial gravity, yet the game's stations hold 2 M people with no mention of spin gravity and treats low g as harmless.

cases.credentials: PhD planetary physics (UCLA); NASA JPL research scientist on the Cassini mission; science advisor to Battlestar Galactica
cases.depiction: Nuclear missiles hit the Cylon Colony, knocking it out of position near a black hole while the fleet holds station amid rocks and gas (finale 'Daybreak')
cases.critique: Nukes striking the hull would vaporize material and impart a change of velocity (Δv) to the Colony; drag from rocks and gas around it would force the ships to keep thrusting to hold attitude and orbit
cases.status_reason: Ablation-driven momentum transfer is the basis of nuclear standoff deflection studies (LLNL 2010s-2020s) and was seen in NASA's DART impact (2022), where ejecta boosted momentum transfer ~3-4x.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics; Directeur de recherche émérite CNRS, Marseille
cases.depiction: A wormhole appears near Saturn, placed there by unknown beings
cases.critique: A natural black hole/wormhole mouth this close is extraordinarily improbable (stellar black holes are ~1e-5 per cubic light-year locally), and a black-hole-mass object at Saturn's distance would wreck the solar system's stability; hence the film's pure-SF choice of an artificially made wormhole
cases.status_reason: Gaia astrometry has since found the nearest dormant black holes (Gaia BH1, 2022) at ~1,560 light-years, consistent with their rarity; a solar-mass-plus object at ~10 AU would strongly perturb planetary orbits.
cases.game_note: No black holes or wormholes in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (University of Florida, 2006); former physics/astronomy professor (Lewis & Clark College, University of Portland); author of Starts With A Bang
cases.depiction: After Kowalski (Clooney) and Stone are snagged by the Soyuz parachute cords near the ISS, Kowalski unclips and drifts away, implying the tether was under tension.
cases.critique: Once the cords are taut, all bodies share the same orbit and velocity, so per Newton's first law there should be essentially no tension; differential atmospheric drag at ISS altitude is far too weak, so Kowalski would not drift away and a gentle tug would have saved him.
cases.status_reason: Co-orbiting bodies in free fall feel no net tension apart from tiny tidal/drag effects, so the scene's dramatic pull is unphysical.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (University of Florida, 2006); former physics/astronomy professor (Lewis & Clark College, University of Portland); author of Starts With A Bang
cases.work: Star Wars: A New Hope / Solo: A Star Wars Story
cases.depiction: Han Solo boasts the Millennium Falcon made the Kessel Run in less than 12 parsecs.
cases.critique: A parsec (~3.26 light-years) is a distance, not a time, so the boast only makes sense as a shorter route; Siegel argues that in general relativity a curved path threading a dense field of low-mass black holes (like a galactic center) could be a shorter, more dangerous route than avoiding them.
cases.status_reason: The parsec-is-distance point is correct, but routes skimming black holes generally increase coordinate travel time (Shapiro delay) rather than yielding shorter-than-straight shortcuts.
cases.game_note: The game uses ly as distance and real star positions; no route-shortening tricks.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (University of Florida, 2006); former physics/astronomy professor (Lewis & Clark College, University of Portland); author of Starts With A Bang
cases.work: Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back
cases.depiction: Massive AT-AT walkers stride across the frozen surface of the ice planet Hoth without breaking through.
cases.critique: Ice load capacity scales roughly as thickness squared (double the thickness, quadruple the load); a ~100+ ton AT-AT needs on the order of 4-5 feet of solid ice, implying Hoth's ice is extremely thick and cold.
cases.status_reason: The thickness-squared bearing-capacity rule (Gold's formula) is standard ice engineering and the estimate is reasonable.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (University of Florida, 2006); former physics/astronomy professor (Lewis & Clark College, University of Portland); author of Starts With A Bang
cases.depiction: The Death Star's superlaser blows up the Earth-like planet Alderaan in seconds.
cases.critique: Unbinding an Earth-like planet takes ~2.2x10^32 J (about a week of the Sun's output); a laser would need to be quadrillions of times more powerful than petawatt lasers and releasing that energy on the station would destroy the Death Star itself; delivering antimatter into the planet's core is the only physically sensible route.
cases.status_reason: The gravitational binding energy figure and the energy-delivery problem are correct order-of-magnitude physics.
cases.game_note: Planets are never destroyed in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (University of Florida, 2006); former physics/astronomy professor (Lewis & Clark College, University of Portland); author of Starts With A Bang
cases.depiction: The plan to save Earth from a 9-km comet is to carve it into many smaller fragments that would supposedly be survivable.
cases.critique: Siegel calls the fragmentation strategy 'simply stupid': 100 small masses at the same speed deliver the same total kinetic energy as one large mass, merely spreading the catastrophe around the globe (as with Shoemaker-Levy 9 at Jupiter); deflection with enough lead time is the right approach.
cases.status_reason: Total energy is conserved, but later terminal-defense studies (e.g., Lubin's PI concept) show that fragmenting into sub-~100 m pieces with adequate lead time turns ground impacts into dispersed airbursts and greatly reduces damage, and debris spreading out also lets part of it miss Earth.
cases.game_note: Kinetic energy is conserved however it is split; the game's 0.9c fleets carry far more yet never threaten planets (5.2).

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (University of Florida, 2006); former physics/astronomy professor (Lewis & Clark College, University of Portland); author of Starts With A Bang
cases.depiction: An artificially arranged octuple star system with the planet Aia (the 'Grief World') sitting at its center.
cases.critique: Multi-star systems are common and septuple systems (AR Cas, Nu Sco) exist, so a natural octuple system is plausible, but a planet at the system's center would sit at an unstable Lagrange-like equilibrium (like L1-L3) and would need active thrusters to stay put.
cases.status_reason: Hierarchical high-multiplicity systems are observed (Gaia-era surveys keep finding 6-7 star systems) and central equilibria in N-body systems are dynamically unstable.
cases.game_note: Multiplicity follows Raghavan+2010 and planets in binaries get a stability cut, so star systems are physically plausible.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (University of Florida, 2006); former physics/astronomy professor (Lewis & Clark College, University of Portland); author of Starts With A Bang
cases.work: Star Trek: Discovery (S1E4 'The Butcher's Knife Cares Not for the Lamb's Cry')
cases.depiction: The ship must avoid a 'Hawking radiation firewall' during a spore jump.
cases.critique: The term mashes together two unrelated black-hole ideas; Hawking radiation from astrophysical black holes is utterly negligible (none will emit enough to ionize an atom for ~10^60 years), so the 'firewall' is nonsense, and a future fleet would have black holes mapped anyway.
cases.status_reason: Hawking temperatures of stellar-mass black holes are ~10^-8 K, far below the CMB; no observable radiation hazard exists.
cases.game_note: No black holes in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (University of Florida, 2006); former physics/astronomy professor (Lewis & Clark College, University of Portland); author of Starts With A Bang
cases.depiction: 'Ripper', a bear-sized tardigrade-like creature, lives and travels through space, feeding on spores.
cases.critique: Real tardigrades are microscopic aquatic animals that only survive vacuum/radiation in a suspended cryptobiotic state; they are not extremophiles that thrive there, so a giant hairy space-faring version is 'science fantasy, not science fiction'.
cases.status_reason: Tardigrade space-exposure experiments (e.g., FOTON-M3) show survival only in dormant tun state, consistent with the critique.
cases.game_note: No space-dwelling creatures in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (University of Florida, 2006); former physics/astronomy professor (Lewis & Clark College, University of Portland); author of Starts With A Bang
cases.work: Star Trek: Discovery (S1E3 'Context Is for Kings')
cases.depiction: Stamets claims there is 'no difference at the quantum level between biology and physics' and links the fungal spore network to the cosmic network of matter and energy.
cases.critique: Shared quantum underpinnings don't erase the distinction between living and non-living systems (which is about energy transport), fungi are evolutionary latecomers rather than cosmic seeds, and mycelial networks have no connection to the cosmic web of matter and dark matter.
cases.status_reason: No known physics couples biological networks to large-scale structure; the cosmic web is governed by gravity on Mpc scales.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (University of Florida, 2006); former physics/astronomy professor (Lewis & Clark College, University of Portland); author of Starts With A Bang
cases.depiction: The spore drive uses a galaxy-spanning mycelial network to jump instantly between distant points.
cases.critique: Mycelium needed billions of years of terrestrial evolution and could not pervade the galaxy, and even entangled spores could not teleport matter or signal faster than light; the concept only works if one adds an extra, traversable spatial dimension.
cases.status_reason: No-communication theorem forbids FTL signaling via entanglement, and LHC and sub-mm gravity tests have found no large traversable extra dimensions.
cases.game_note: No FTL jumps in the game (apart from the instant refugee transfer leak, 2.8i).

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (University of Florida, 2006); former physics/astronomy professor (Lewis & Clark College, University of Portland); author of Starts With A Bang
cases.depiction: Discovery is stranded in the Mirror Universe, a parallel universe populated by the same people and ships.
cases.critique: Parallel universes have a basis in the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics and the show handles them 'plausibly enough', but it is implausible that so much (same people, personalities, ships) would be identical across branches.

cases.status_reason: Density and contact-pressure arithmetic is sound given mass conservation; the films are inconsistent about shrinking mass.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

cases.status_reason: Kepler/Newton orbital dynamics: tangential Δv changes orbital shape, not speed at fixed radius.
cases.game_note: No orbital manoeuvres in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.status_reason: a=ω²R; the depiction is self-consistent (structural strength aside).
cases.game_note: Spin habitats are not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
cases.depiction: Discovery One's crew live in a centrifuge inside the crew sphere producing Earth-like gravity.

cases.status_reason: Gravity gradient and Coriolis effects scale inversely with radius; small centrifuges are problematic.
cases.game_note: Spin habitats are not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

cases.status_reason: Solar flux (~1.4 kW/m^2) and ion-thruster physics give tiny thrust-to-mass ratios.
cases.game_note: Ship power systems are not depicted; propulsion energy is supplied by external lasers.

cases.credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

cases.status_reason: Centripetal acceleration estimate and human g-tolerance (~9 g with g-suits) are standard.
cases.game_note: G's instant 0 to 0.95c acceleration implies unlimited g, far beyond the film's 12.6 g.

cases.status_reason: Momentum/angular-momentum reasoning is sound, but assumes the absorbed stellar matter carries the orbital angular momentum into planetary spin; a planet holding a solar mass would actually collapse.

cases.status_reason: Momentum conservation; Newton's third law gives equal recoil to the shooter.
cases.game_note: No hand weapons in the game.

cases.status_reason: Quantum tunnelling and superposition are real only at microscopic scales; decoherence rules out macroscopic multi-location; quantum 'teleportation' transfers states, not matter.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.status_reason: Alcubierre geometry is a valid GR solution, but superluminal versions still require negative energy density and face causality/horizon problems; 2021 'positive-energy' warp proposals are subluminal.

cases.critique: Human body (~1000 kg/m^3) in molten rock (~3300 kg/m^3) would float once a third submerged; also gravity at that depth is ~20% weaker (g scales with r inside a uniform sphere), which the film ignores.
cases.status_reason: Archimedes' principle is clear; the uniform-density gravity estimate is crude (Earth's real g rises slightly into the mantle) but buoyancy point stands.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.physicist: Costas J. Efthimiou & Ralph A. Llewellyn
cases.credentials: Efthimiou: PhD physics, Professor, UCF; Llewellyn: PhD physics, Professor Emeritus, UCF
cases.depiction: Superman flies around Earth so fast that Earth's rotation reverses, turning back time to save Lois Lane.
cases.critique: Earth's rotation has no link to the flow of time; in vacuum Superman has nothing to push against; he flies the wrong direction (his reaction would speed Earth up); and absorbing Earth's angular momentum would require near light speed at a radius >2.3e23 m.
cases.status_reason: Angular momentum conservation and Newton's third law make the feat impossible as shown; time direction is set by entropy, not Earth's spin.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.critique: Moving ~4e8 kg at ~10 m/s needs ~2e10 J; from food energy Magneto would burn ~1,350 lb of fat; even with mass-energy conversion his ~37 MW output would make him glow ~926 times brighter than a 60 W bulb; and cutting the suspension cables would collapse the deck.
cases.status_reason: Energy bookkeeping is correct to order of magnitude; biological power output is limited to hundreds of watts.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.physicist: Costas J. Efthimiou & Ralph A. Llewellyn

cases.critique: In Celsius (the script's units) -300 C is below absolute zero; in Fahrenheit 700 F cannot cremate a body in seconds (cremation needs ~1000 C for 1-2 h); a ~10 g water film on his head would evaporate in <9 s under Mercury-like insolation, and the planet should have lost its atmosphere.
cases.status_reason: Absolute zero (-273.15 C) is inviolable; latent-heat and insolation estimates are sound.
cases.game_note: Not depicted; game temperatures are equilibrium values in kelvin.

cases.critique: Nothing supplies the impulse to stop her forward momentum except foot friction, whose torque adds to gravity's and tips her onto the blades; with her center of mass outside her base of support the pose is not an equilibrium.
cases.status_reason: Standard impulse, torque and static-equilibrium analysis; internal muscle torques cannot move the center of mass.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.status_reason: Froude-number gait scaling is well supported by reduced-gravity experiments and Apollo footage.
cases.game_note: Low gravity changes how humans function; the game treats 0.1 g worlds as fully settleable with no effects on people.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Univ. of Colorado Boulder); astronomy educator and textbook author (The Cosmic Perspective; What Is Relativity?, Columbia UP 2014)
cases.depiction: Habitable, Earth-like planets (Miller's, Mann's, Edmunds') orbit the supermassive black hole Gargantua, warmed by its accretion disk.
cases.critique: 'Probably not real': heat and light would come from the accretion disk, which emits mostly high-energy (X-ray/UV) radiation, making habitable conditions implausible.
cases.status_reason: Typical disks emit X-rays/UV, but the film posits an unusually cool, quiescent disk, and later work (e.g. Schnittman 2019) shows habitability near SMBHs is not strictly ruled out, though extreme blueshift/radiation problems remain.
cases.game_note: No black-hole-lit planets in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Univ. of Colorado Boulder); author of What Is Relativity?
cases.depiction: Miller's planet has a shallow ocean swept by kilometer-high waves.
cases.critique: Huge waves in a very shallow ocean seem unrealistic (though less important than whether the planets could exist at all).
cases.status_reason: Ordinary wind waves cannot be that tall in shallow water, but the film's rationale (tidal bores from a planet rocking in Gargantua's tidal field) is a debated but not impossible mechanism.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Univ. of Colorado Boulder); author of What Is Relativity?
cases.depiction: A wormhole near Saturn lets the crew reach another galaxy.
cases.critique: Wormholes arise from general relativity's equations, but 'there is no known way to make a stable wormhole' people could travel through; this element is speculative (unlike the film's time dilation and black-hole visuals, which he calls real science).
cases.status_reason: Traversable wormholes still require exotic negative-energy matter in 2026; none is known to exist.
cases.game_note: No wormholes in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Univ. of Cambridge); astrophysicist, Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (Chandra X-ray Center)

cases.critique: In reality Hubble (28.5° inclination) and ISS (51.6°) are in very different orbits; the film only works if one invents a backstory in which Hubble's inclination and altitude were changed and the ISS raised ~200 km ('retconning' needed to make HST MMU-accessible).
cases.status_reason: Plane changes cost delta-v ~ 2v sin(Δi/2), ~3 km/s for 23°, far beyond any jetpack; real orbits are as he states.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astrophysics (Univ. of Cambridge); Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics

cases.critique: A debris field moving slowly relative to the ISS, dense, thin and repeatedly returning must share nearly the ISS's orbital period and span hundreds of km; 'None of this makes sense with the Russian military test explanation'—the source would have to be something co-orbiting like a cargo ship.
cases.status_reason: Debris from a distant ASAT test would be in different orbits with large relative velocities and would disperse, not return as a coherent cloud.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Doctor of Physical and Mathematical Sciences; leading researcher, Laboratory of Stellar Physics, Pulkovo Observatory (known for the 'Krasnikov tube' spacetime)
cases.depiction: 'Inverted' people and objects have reversed entropy and move backward in time among normal ones (e.g. wind hitting an inverted person's back).
cases.critique: The film's 'inversion' is reversal of the arrow of time; reversed entropy as Nolan presents it is illogical and impossible, and details like the wind contradict common sense. No known law forbids a region with a reversed arrow of time, but it would look like a 'miracle'; the realistic time-machine concept is the Morris-Thorne moving wormhole.
cases.status_reason: Entropy's arrow is statistical and tied to cosmological low-entropy initial conditions; locally reversed objects interacting with normal surroundings would be overwhelmingly improbable.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (UCLA); Professor of Planetary Science, Univ. of Arizona/UCLA; PI of NASA NEOWISE and NEO Surveyor; science advisor to the film
cases.depiction: A newly discovered planet-killing comet will hit Earth only months after detection.
cases.critique: Short warning times are realistic for long-period comets (cf. Comet NEOWISE 2020: months from discovery to closest approach) because surveys have catalogued most large near-Earth asteroids but a much smaller fraction of comets; but no known asteroid or comet is on an impact trajectory, so the premise is fiction.
cases.status_reason: Long-period comets arrive with months of warning and remain the hardest impact threat to catalog; no known >1 km impactor exists.
cases.game_note: No comet detection in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD (Cornell, astronomy/planetary science); planetary scientist, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, specialist in Martian dust storms
cases.depiction: A violent Martian dust storm topples the ascent vehicle, impales Watney with debris and forces evacuation.
cases.critique: Martian air has ~1% of Earth's density, so a 60 mph wind feels like ~6 mph: 'you would probably feel a breeze, but it wouldn't be knocking you over,' though real dust storms are dramatic and have consequences (e.g. for solar power).
cases.status_reason: Dynamic pressure scales with density x v^2; Mars' ~0.6 kPa atmosphere cannot exert the forces shown.
cases.game_note: Weather is not modelled.

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (Caltech); Senior Astronomer, SETI Institute
cases.depiction: SETI researchers detect the aliens' signal and enormous alien ships cross interstellar space to attack Earth.
cases.critique: The SETI premise is broadly right ('We are looking for the aliens'), but interstellar travel is enormously expensive—'Our fastest rocket would take almost 100,000 years' to reach the nearest star—and there is little motive to come 'just to flatten the White House'.
cases.status_reason: At ~17 km/s (Voyager), 4.2 ly takes ~75,000 years; interstellar energy costs scale with kinetic energy of huge masses.
cases.game_note: Fleets, cargo and settlers pay for interstellar travel (4.2, 4.10), but pirates appear at colonies with no origin, travel or energy cost (5.5).

cases.credentials: PhD astronomy (Caltech); Senior Astronomer, SETI Institute; science consultant on the film

cases.critique: Arriving that quickly is implausible: without faster-than-light travel the round trip (signal out, ships back) would take closer to a thousand years; any species that could do it would be vastly more advanced than us.
cases.status_reason: A 7-year signal-plus-travel round trip limits the source to <3.5 ly even at light speed, and no star lies that close.
cases.game_note: Orders and fleets respect light delay and 0.9c travel, but pirates materialise from nowhere (5.5) and accepted refugees are teleported instantly (2.8i).

cases.status_reason: With relative motion arrested and no thrust, nothing separates them; tidal/differential orbital effects over seconds are negligible.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.critique: 'Probably not real': oxygen is highly reactive, so breathable levels would likely require photosynthesis or a similar ongoing process.
cases.status_reason: Abiotic O2 build-up (e.g. via water photolysis and hydrogen escape) is now modelled as possible, though Earth-like breathable levels without life remain unlikely.
cases.game_note: Atmospheric composition is not modelled (only pressure and temperature).

cases.status_reason: Spin gravity follows a = omega^2 r; Cassini took ~7 years with gravity assists, but a ~2-year transfer is feasible with higher delta-v.

cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Astronomer (radio astronomy, Milky Way), Professor, Faculty of Science, Kagoshima University; science adviser for Yamato 2199

cases.status_reason: HII-region densities (~10^2-10^4 cm^-3) are ~15+ orders of magnitude below air; ram pressure on a ship is negligible.
cases.game_note: The game uses a Tarantula Nebula image (an extragalactic false-colour object) as a backdrop for nearby star systems.

cases.status_reason: GM☉M⊕/2a ≈ 2.65×10^33 J is correct; the energy scale is indeed prohibitive.
cases.game_note: Planets are never moved in the game.

cases.credentials: Research Fellow, China Academy of Engineering Physics (nuclear materials/physics)

cases.critique: Fusion joins light nuclei; elements above Z≈90 tend to fission and below Z≈10 to fuse, so fusion of heavy nuclei has no theory or means of realization and exists only in SF.
cases.status_reason: Fusion is exothermic up to iron (stars burn C, O, Si), so 'heavy' fusion of rock elements is not forbidden in principle, though wildly beyond any achievable confinement conditions.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.status_reason: Jupiter's atmosphere lacks the density/temperature confinement for self-sustaining fusion; laser ICF works only on compressed mm-scale pellets, so no laser could 'ignite' Jupiter.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Research Professor, National Astronomical Observatories CAS (black holes, gamma-ray bursts; PhD); science adviser to The Wandering Earth 2
cases.depiction: Proxima Centauri chosen as Earth's new 'sun'
cases.critique: Proxima is a red dwarf (~1/7 solar mass) chosen only for proximity; its habitable zone is very close and its flares are far more violent (2017 flare 10x strongest solar flare, Proxima b gets ~4000x Earth's radiation), so it is not a good second sun.
cases.status_reason: Proxima's frequent superflares and close-in HZ remain the main habitability concerns in 2026 literature.
cases.game_note: M-dwarf flares and close-in HZs threaten habitability, but the game gives Proxima d a 3.3 atm ocean world with natives, models no atmospheric escape, and G has no flares at all.

cases.status_reason: Lunar gravitational binding energy ~1.2×10^29 J vs global arsenal ~10^19 J.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.critique: Using fusion energy to push Earth 'makes sense in principle', but the film's heavy-nucleus fusion is far harder than the D-T light-nucleus fusion being researched; fusion propulsion of planets is 'premature'.
cases.status_reason: Ignition conditions scale steeply with Coulomb barrier; heavy-element fusion requires stellar-core conditions.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Research Professor, China Institute of Atomic Energy; chief scientist of JUNA nuclear astrophysics experiment (PhD)

cases.critique: Not feasible in the strict sense: the general direction is right, but the Sun's gravity is too small and the novel exaggerates the effect by about 10^8.
cases.status_reason: No known solar mechanism amplifies radio by the required factors; solar gravitational lensing needs a receiver/transmitter at ≥550 AU.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.critique: Argued that Earth-size or larger planets of roughly equal mass cannot form a true double planet: over tens of millions of years the orbit would become unstable and they would escape or collide and coalesce.
cases.status_reason: An isolated, mutually tidally locked binary planet is a stable two-body system (cf. Pluto-Charon); such pairs are rare from formation, not dynamically forbidden.
cases.game_note: No double planets in the game.

cases.credentials: PhD (Virginia Tech); Assistant Professor/PI, Laboratory for Dark Matter and Neutrino, Westlake University (experimental particle physics); homework hosted on his lab's teaching site for General Physics I
cases.depiction: Earth, captured by Jupiter, approaches Jupiter's Roche limit and risks being torn apart before impact
cases.critique: Homework problem: using densities (Earth 5.5, Jupiter 1.3 g/cm^3) a surface rock remains bound until d < R_J, so Earth would not be disintegrated before hitting Jupiter; 'the movie director should take our class in advance to avoid a mistake' (plot not in Liu Cixin's novel).
cases.status_reason: The rigid-rock estimate gives ~0.8 R_J, but a planet-sized body behaves as a self-gravitating fluid whose Roche limit (~1.5 R_J) lies outside Jupiter, so tidal disruption before impact is plausible.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Astronomer, researcher at Yonsei University Galaxy Evolution Research Center (doctoral-level researcher in galaxy evolution; science communicator) — PhD status at time not confirmed
cases.depiction: Crews manually collect orbital debris by flying out and grabbing it
cases.critique: Manual collection is impractical: debris moves at orbital speeds and the collector must match each piece's relative velocity, which is dangerous and uneconomical; systematic approaches (deorbit, active removal) are needed.
cases.status_reason: Rendezvous with each object costs large delta-v; real ADR missions (e.g., ClearSpace, ADRAS-J) target one large object per mission.
cases.game_note: No orbital debris in the game.

cases.credentials: Professor, College of Physics and Electrical Engineering, Anyang Normal University (theoretical physics, celestial mechanics)

cases.critique: Peer-reviewed College Physics (大学物理) paper: using angular-momentum conservation, the work-energy theorem and first cosmic velocity, stopping Earth's spin needs at least ~4.1×10^30 J, and discusses its (in)feasibility as an energy budget.
cases.status_reason: Earth's rotational KE alone is ~2.1×10^29 J; including exhaust energy a ~10^30 J budget is plausible and far beyond human energy production.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Professor, College of Physics and Electrical Engineering, Anyang Normal University (theoretical physics, celestial mechanics)
cases.depiction: Step two: planetary engines drive Earth out of the Solar System while keeping enough mass for life
cases.critique: Follow-up College Physics paper: using momentum conservation, escape velocity and an effective exhaust velocity, the minimum work to remove Earth from the Solar System is ~2.72×10^32 J; feasibility discussed from an energy standpoint.
cases.status_reason: Infeasibility conclusion stands, but the figure is ~10x below Earth's orbital binding energy (~2.65×10^33 J) and hinges on exhaust/gravity-assist accounting.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Professor, Graduate School of Engineering, Tohoku University (plasma science, PhD)
cases.work: Mobile Suit Gundam series (機動戦士ガンダム)

cases.critique: In 『機動戦士ガンダム 宇宙世紀vs.現代科学』 analyses the beam saber as plasma and suggests blade colour differences reflect the different gases each side could obtain; distinguishes beams, lasers and mega-particle cannons.
cases.status_reason: Plasma colour from gas emission lines is real physics, but a self-confined, fixed-length plasma blade has no known confinement mechanism.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Particle physicist, Nagoya University (Institute for Advanced Research / Graduate School of Science)
cases.work: Mobile Suit Gundam series (機動戦士ガンダム)

cases.critique: In 『機動戦士ガンダム 宇宙世紀vs.現代科学』 argues that if Minovsky particles are treated as a type of dark matter, some of their properties become consistent.
cases.status_reason: Dark-matter candidates by definition barely interact electromagnetically, so they could not jam radar; only exotic dark-sector models (e.g., dark photons) offer a partial link.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Researcher, Helical Research Division, National Institute for Fusion Science (fusion/plasma simulation, PhD)
cases.work: Mobile Suit Gundam series (機動戦士ガンダム)

cases.status_reason: He-3 abundance claims are correct and D-He3 is aneutronic-leaning, but it needs ~several times higher temperatures than D-T and no reactor has achieved it.
cases.game_note: The game's energy comes from Dyson swarms, not fusion fuel.

cases.credentials: Research Professor, National Astronomical Observatories CAS; Professor of Astronomy, University of CAS (black-hole astrophysics, PhD)
cases.depiction: Equatorial steering engines (150 trillion tonnes thrust each) stop Earth's rotation
cases.critique: Earth's rotational energy is ~2.24×10^29 J (~10^12 Tsar Bombas); a single engine would decelerate the 460 m/s equatorial spin at ~2.5×10^-7 m/s², taking ~60 years; even ~100 continuous, equal engines make it nearly impossible for humans.
cases.status_reason: Iω²/2 ≈ 2.1-2.2×10^29 J is the standard value; the energy/thrust scales are far beyond any technology.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Research Professor, NAOC; Professor, University of CAS
cases.depiction: Surface cities and engines survive after Earth's rotation is halted
cases.critique: Without rotation the oceans would migrate poleward (submerging most continents, leaving an equatorial supercontinent), and loss of equatorial centrifugal support could collapse plates, causing global earthquakes and tsunamis; surface cities and engines would likely not survive, so the film's underground cities are more plausible.
cases.status_reason: The ~21 km equatorial bulge and ocean geoid are set by rotation; despinning redistributes water and stresses the lithosphere.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Research Professor, NAOC; Professor, University of CAS
cases.depiction: Earth keeps its atmosphere during the journey after rotation stops
cases.critique: If rotation between core and mantle stops, the geomagnetic field may vanish and the solar wind could strip the atmosphere as happened on Mars (now ~1% of Earth's).
cases.status_reason: Dynamo weakening without rotation is plausible, but solar-wind stripping acts over hundreds of Myr, negligible on the film's ~centuries timescale (and Earth moves away from the Sun).
cases.game_note: Atmospheric loss to stellar wind and flares is not modelled; close-in M-dwarf planets keep random thick atmospheres (Proxima d with 3.3 atm).

cases.credentials: Research Professor, NAOC; Professor, University of CAS
cases.depiction: Igniting Jupiter's hydrogen with Earth's atmospheric oxygen so the explosion's shock wave pushes Earth out of Jupiter's grip
cases.critique: Earth's oxygen would not mix well enough with Jupiter's hydrogen to burn; even if it did, the chemical energy and resulting shock would be weaker than the solar wind, which Earth's magnetosphere deflects, so it could not push Earth away (at most stripping some atmosphere).
cases.status_reason: Chemical combustion energy of any feasible mixed volume is negligible versus the momentum change needed for Earth (~10^28 kg·m/s scale).
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Research Professor, NAOC; Professor, University of CAS
cases.depiction: Earth's long voyage to Proxima Centauri
cases.critique: Listed crossing the asteroid belt, Kuiper belt and Oort cloud (which extends ~halfway to Proxima) as a major collision-risk challenge for the wandering Earth.
cases.status_reason: These reservoirs are extremely sparse: Earth's swept volume through the Oort cloud gives an expected impact count ~10^-6, so collisions are not a significant risk.
cases.game_note: The game correctly treats interstellar space as empty of collision hazards (only dust dose in S).

cases.credentials: Research Professor, NAOC; Professor, University of CAS
cases.depiction: The Sun exhausts core hydrogen, undergoes a helium flash and expands, forcing Earth to flee
cases.critique: States that helium ignition after core-hydrogen exhaustion releasing more heat and expanding the Sun is 'fully consistent with our scientific understanding' (the film's accurate science).
cases.status_reason: The sequence is real, but for the Sun it lies ~5 Gyr ahead (not within centuries), and the core flash itself is invisible at the surface.
cases.game_note: Stars are static in the game, which is correct on its 500-year timescale.

cases.credentials: Professor, School of Astronomy and Space Science, Nanjing University (celestial mechanics, PhD); science adviser to the TV series
cases.depiction: Signal timing in Ye Wenjie's discovery: radiation from Jupiter reaching Earth directly vs. via the Sun
cases.critique: Verified with the cosine rule and 1970s planetary data that the direct Jupiter-Earth light-travel time is ~2099 s and via the Sun ~3101 s (difference ~16 min 42 s), matching the novel; noted that using modern ephemerides for the story's era would be an anachronism.
cases.status_reason: Simple light-travel geometry; 2099 s ↔ ~4.2 AU Earth-Jupiter distance, consistent with orbital geometry.
cases.game_note: Light takes tens of minutes across a planetary system, and up to ~2 months to Proxima within the alpha Cen system, yet the game sets light delay to 0 inside a system (a minor simplification).

cases.credentials: Astronomer, Professor, Kagoshima University; Yamato 2199 science adviser
cases.work: Space Battleship Yamato 2199 (宇宙戦艦ヤマト2199)
cases.depiction: Ep.8: a giant arch-shaped prominence/flare on the red dwarf Gliese 581 threatens the ship
cases.critique: An arch-shaped plasma prominence is plausible, and red dwarfs are known to produce huge flares that can exceed the Sun's.
cases.status_reason: M-dwarf superflares (TESS/Kepler statistics) routinely exceed the largest solar flares in relative and often absolute energy.
cases.game_note: S models TESS-based M-dwarf flares and surface dose correctly, but G has no flares or radiation at all.

cases.credentials: Astronomer, Professor, Kagoshima University; Yamato 2199 science adviser
cases.work: Space Battleship Yamato 2199 (宇宙戦艦ヤマト2199)
cases.depiction: Ep.13: Yamato hides inside a young star's protoplanetary (accretion) disk where dust coalesces into planetesimals
cases.critique: The depiction of dust coalescing into planetesimals in a young star's disk matches the standard planet-formation picture for the early Solar System (~4.6-5 Gyr ago), building on the 1980s Kyoto model.
cases.status_reason: ALMA disk images (e.g., HL Tau) and the Kyoto (Hayashi) model remain the basis of planet-formation theory, though pebble accretion now supplements it.
cases.game_note: Planet formation is not simulated (planets are drawn from statistics, 7.6).

cases.credentials: Astronomer, Professor, Kagoshima University; Yamato 2199 science adviser
cases.work: Space Battleship Yamato 2199 (宇宙戦艦ヤマト2199)
cases.depiction: Ep.15: the fictional neutron star 'Karel 163' whose beams sweep space and disturb the warp
cases.critique: The name is fictional but neutron stars are real supernova remnants with intense magnetic fields and fast rotation, whose beams sweep space like a lighthouse, as depicted.
cases.status_reason: Pulsar lighthouse model of rotating, magnetized neutron stars is well established.
cases.game_note: No neutron stars in the game.

cases.credentials: Professor, Department of Physics and Informatics, Faculty of Science, Yamaguchi University (general relativity/cosmology, PhD)
cases.depiction: Doraemon's time machine (travel to the future and past)
cases.critique: In a university lecture titled 「相対性理論でドラえもんの世界が現実に？」: relativity does allow travel to the future like a time machine (moving near light speed slows time), but no method for travelling to the past has been found.
cases.status_reason: Kinematic time dilation is experimentally verified; past-directed travel needs CTCs/exotic matter with no known realization.
cases.game_note: Near-light travel is a one-way trip into the future, but the game never shows travellers' proper time.

cases.credentials: Nuclear physicist, PhD; Director, RIKEN Nishina Center for Accelerator-Based Science (team that synthesized nihonium)
cases.work: Shin Ultraman (シン・ウルトラマン)
cases.depiction: 'Specium' (スペシウム), the alien element powering Ultraman
cases.critique: Offered a 'reading' of Specium as element 133, linking it to the predicted 'island of stability' of long-lived superheavy nuclei.
cases.status_reason: The island of stability is predicted near Z≈114-126 (N≈184); Z=133 lies beyond current predictions, so long life is speculative.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Research Professor, Institute of High Energy Physics, CAS (astrophysicist, PhD)
cases.depiction: An astronaut sacrifices himself by ramming the space station into Jupiter's atmosphere to ignite it
cases.critique: Called it scientifically unreasonable: mature technology such as intercontinental ballistic missiles could have delivered the ignition instead of sacrificing an astronaut.
cases.status_reason: An uncrewed delivery is sensible, but the Earth-Jupiter gap (~70,000 km) exceeds ICBM capability and the underlying ignition mechanism fails regardless.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Astronomer (celestial mechanics), Hatanaka group, Department of Astronomy, University of Tokyo; later professor
cases.depiction: Rocket engines at the South Pole move Earth out of the path of the dense star Gorath, which swallows the Moon instead
cases.critique: As consultant he computed the force, momentum and energy needed to move Earth (assuming it feasible) but objected that if the Moon were swallowed by Gorath, Earth would have been swallowed too, asking that publicity note this part was a 'lie'.
cases.status_reason: With Gorath ~6000 Earth masses, an encounter close enough to capture the Moon would devastate Earth only ~384,000 km away; differential capture is implausible.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD (science), Director, Amanogawa Galaxy Astronomy Research Center, Kagoshima University; Yamato 2199 science adviser
cases.work: Space Battleship Yamato (宇宙戦艦ヤマト series, incl. 2199/2202)
cases.depiction: Warp navigation lets Yamato cross 168,000 light years
cases.critique: No known real-world physics allows warp; a story that uses it must supply its own 'SF logic', and the energy source alone would not suffice—a separate FTL mechanism is needed.
cases.status_reason: Warp metrics (Alcubierre, Lentz) require negative energy or unphysical energy conditions; no viable mechanism exists in 2026.
cases.game_note: The game has no warp; it plays out the sub-light alternative.

cases.credentials: PhD (science), Kagoshima University; Yamato 2199 science adviser
cases.work: Space Battleship Yamato (宇宙戦艦ヤマト series)
cases.depiction: Without warp, the journey to the Large Magellanic Cloud and back
cases.critique: Even at near light speed the crew would age less, but people at home experience normal time: a 160,000-light-year round trip would take 320,000 years for Earth.
cases.status_reason: Special relativity: Earth-frame round-trip time ≥ 2d/c.
cases.game_note: Earth-frame times are shown correctly, but the crew's shorter proper time is never displayed.

cases.credentials: PhD (science), Kagoshima University; Yamato 2199 science adviser
cases.work: Space Battleship Yamato (宇宙戦艦ヤマト series)
cases.depiction: Communication between Yamato and Earth across interstellar distances
cases.critique: Radio from 15 light-years away means a 30-year wait for a reply, so FTL communication (and warp) is essential for such stories.
cases.status_reason: Signal round-trip time = 2d/c; no FTL signalling is allowed by relativity or entanglement.
cases.game_note: The game embraces this: orders and replies travel at c, so a colony 15 ly away answers in 30 years.

cases.credentials: PhD (science), Kagoshima University; Yamato 2199 science adviser
cases.work: Space Battleship Yamato 2199 (宇宙戦艦ヤマト2199)
cases.depiction: Yamato launching directly from Earth's surface, and crew moving normally aboard
cases.critique: Spaceships cannot launch like this; the story needs to explain artificial gravity / 'inertial control' for it to make sense.
cases.status_reason: A vehicle with thrust/weight >1 can lift off, so launch per se is possible; the unexplained power, ship structure and crew acceleration are the real problems.
cases.game_note: G ships also need unexplained 'inertial control': they go 0 to 0.95c instantly with crews aboard.

cases.credentials: PhD (science), Kagoshima University; Yamato 2199 science adviser
cases.work: Space Battleship Yamato 2199 (宇宙戦艦ヤマト2199)
cases.depiction: Crew running normally on the surface of Enceladus
cases.critique: Enceladus's gravity is tiny (quoted as ~0.7% of the Moon's), so running as shown in 2199 is wrong.
cases.status_reason: Conclusion correct (g≈0.11 m/s², ~1.2% of Earth's), but that is ~7% of the Moon's, not 0.7% (possibly a translation slip).
cases.game_note: The game computes surface gravity correctly from mass and radius.

cases.credentials: Astronomer, PhD; Associate Professor and Public Relations Director, Astronomy Information Center, National Astronomical Observatory of Japan (supernovae/transients)
cases.work: Space Battleship Yamato (宇宙戦艦ヤマト series)
cases.depiction: Warp navigation that bends space-time rather than accelerating the ship
cases.critique: Warp that 'bends space-time' is a different theory from ship propulsion and is 'the right direction' for FTL travel.
cases.status_reason: Spacetime-geometry approaches (Alcubierre-type) are the only GR-consistent FTL concepts, but all require negative energy and remain unrealizable.
cases.game_note: No warp in the game.

cases.credentials: Research Professor, NAOC; Professor of Astronomy, University of CAS (PhD)
cases.depiction: Using Jupiter's gravity as a slingshot to accelerate Earth
cases.critique: The gravitational-slingshot principle is sound and routinely used by probes (e.g., Voyager 1 at Jupiter and Saturn), explained via a ball bouncing off a moving train.
cases.status_reason: Gravity assists exchange momentum with the planet in the heliocentric frame; standard mission design.
cases.game_note: No gravity assists in the game.

cases.credentials: Research Professor, NAOC; Professor of Astronomy, University of CAS (PhD)
cases.depiction: Earth drifting inside Jupiter's Roche limit and facing tidal break-up
cases.critique: Within the (rigid) Roche limit Jupiter's tides would tear Earth apart, so the film's crossing of the limit is a genuine threat, motivating the evacuation plan.
cases.status_reason: Tidal disruption is real for a self-gravitating planet (fluid limit ~1.5 R_J), but the rigid-body Roche limit (~0.8 R_J) lies inside Jupiter, so the 'rigid' framing is inconsistent.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Senior Engineer (正高级工程师, full-professor rank), National Center for Nanoscience and Technology, China — PhD/physics degree not confirmed
cases.depiction: The 'Droplet' (水滴) probe whose hull is bound by the strong interaction, perfectly smooth and droplet-shaped
cases.critique: Only an extremely dense material could be built with the strong interaction; at macroscopic size its own gravity and other effects could not be ignored, so it would not hold a mirror-perfect droplet shape.
cases.status_reason: Strong-force-bound matter has nuclear density (~2×10^17 kg/m^3); a metre-scale droplet would weigh ~10^17 kg and collapse/crush under self-gravity.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Senior Engineer (正高级工程师), National Center for Nanoscience and Technology — PhD/physics degree not confirmed
cases.depiction: 'Flying Blade' (飞刃) nanofilaments slicing the ship Judgment Day in Operation Guzheng
cases.critique: The closest real material is carbon nanotubes, the strongest known, but still far from strong enough to cut a ship; a space elevator is more feasible than the nano-blade.
cases.status_reason: Macroscopic CNT fibres are far weaker than ideal; but cutting is governed by stress concentration, so an ideal ~100 GPa filament could plausibly slice steel—the main obstacle is manufacturing length.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: PhD in experimental physics, MIT (1993), MIT postdoc; founder/CEO of Sohu; gives regular public physics lectures
cases.depiction: After Earth's rotation is halted, ocean water shifts and floods cities such as Beijing
cases.critique: In a public discussion with director Frant Gwo he worked through the physics of equatorial water surging toward the poles once rotation stops (explaining the flooding), plus how Earth is propelled after stopping, planetary distances and orbital speeds.
cases.status_reason: Removing centrifugal support collapses the ~21 km equatorial bulge of the geoid; oceans redistribute toward the poles, flooding mid/high-latitude land.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Professor, University of Science and Technology of China (quantum information/semiconductor qubits, PhD); secretary-general, CCF Quantum Computing Committee
cases.depiction: The 550-series quantum computers (550W/MOSS) with enormous computing power
cases.critique: Judged the film's 550 series to be, in effect, already 'an excellent universal (general-purpose) quantum computer', far beyond today's devices, while expecting quantum computing to matter in future production and life.
cases.status_reason: Fault-tolerant universal quantum computing remains undemonstrated in 2026 (best systems are ~100-1000 noisy/early logical qubits), and quantum hardware confers no 'self-awareness'.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Research Professor, NAOC; Professor of Astronomy, University of CAS (PhD)
cases.depiction: Day and night on an Earth whose rotation has been stopped
cases.critique: Stated that a non-rotating Earth would keep one face toward the Sun with the other in permanent night (like polar day/night), leaving the dark side too cold for life.
cases.status_reason: A planet with zero sidereal spin still sees the Sun circle once per orbit (half-year day/night), so it is not tidally locked; extreme hemispheric temperature swings would still result.
cases.game_note: Rotation sets day/night climate, but the game's tidally locked planets have no day/night contrast (the lock is a display label only).

cases.credentials: Professor, Department of Physics and Informatics, Faculty of Science, Yamaguchi University (general relativity/cosmology, PhD)
cases.depiction: The 4D pocket (四次元ポケット) holding a vast space inside a small pouch
cases.critique: Notes that spacetime structures 'like Doraemon's pocket'—reproducing an infinitely large space inside a finite lab region, e.g., creating a small universe by inflating an early-universe state—are being studied theoretically, though realization is far off.
cases.status_reason: GR permits 'bag-of-gold'/baby-universe geometries (Farhi-Guth-Guven), but they need energy densities and quantum tunnelling far beyond any lab, and remain purely theoretical.
cases.game_note: Not depicted.

cases.credentials: Astrophysicist, D.Sc. Kyoto University; Professor, Osaka Kyoiku University
cases.work: Mobile Suit Gundam: Char's Counterattack (機動戦士ガンダム 逆襲のシャア)
cases.depiction: Colony drops and the attempted Axis asteroid drop to plunge Earth into a 'nuclear winter' cooling (地球寒冷化作戦)
cases.critique: In a 2010 seminar shared with Tomino and Fukui ('ガンダム天文入門') he framed the colony/Axis drop as a 'dinosaur winter', relating it to the Chicxulub impact and Alvarez hypothesis, arguing large impacts genuinely cause global cooling and mass extinction (and that eventual real impacts motivate space migration).
cases.status_reason: Chicxulub impact winter (soot/sulfate aerosols) is the accepted cause of the K-Pg extinction; a multi-km Axis impact would produce comparable global cooling.
cases.game_note: Large impacts devastate planets via impact winter; the game's 0.9c fleets carry ~5e4 Chicxulubs of KE yet never threaten worlds.

cases.credentials: Astronomer, Professor, Kagoshima University; Yamato 2199 science adviser
cases.work: Space Battleship Yamato 2199 (宇宙戦艦ヤマト2199)
cases.depiction: Rogue (free-floating) planets with no host star encountered during the voyage
cases.critique: Rogue planets without a parent star are real, having been confirmed through infrared observations and gravitational microlensing.
cases.status_reason: Microlensing surveys (OGLE, MOA) and JWST imaging have since confirmed abundant free-floating planets, down to Earth mass.
cases.game_note: No rogue planets in the game.
